name: Lena Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Lena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the corrugator at a cardboard box plant, by the river. The corrugator's a machine as long as a swimming pool. It takes big rolls of paper, crimps one into waves, glues it between two flat sheets with starch and heat, and cuts it into board. I'm on days, six to two, and I'm the one who sets the glue gap and the steam, and the one who gets called when a roll splices badly and the whole thing jams.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's mine, in a way. Nineteen years on that machine. I know when the paper's damp just by the sound it makes going over the rolls. What wears me out is the heat in summer, and that the pay hasn't kept up, we're a bit below other plants. But there are no other plants nearby, so that's that. Paul drives the school bus, so between us we manage, just.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, nothing to worry about after all. I'm not one for posting online. At work I'd probably just shrug, and somebody would make a joke about the computer that couldn't fold a box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd suit me fine. I don't use any of those AI things, my daughter does, I don't. If it all fizzles, I keep doing what I know, and that's what I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. Same shifts, same machine. Maybe finally ask about the senior pay grade I keep getting told is coming next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, really, though I wasn't that worried in the first place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the senior pay grade keeps coming next year. How long has that been going on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years. Every review, my manager says, Lena, you're the best on that machine, next year for sure. I'm starting to think next year is a place, not a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If things carry on as they are, what's the thing about money that bothers you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we've got nothing put by. If Paul's bus breaks down, he doesn't get paid, he's on a contract. Last winter he lost a week to a gearbox, and we lived on pasta and borrowed from my sister. I hate borrowing.

S0.say: I'd say there you go, nothing to worry about after all. I don't post online, and at work I'd just shrug along with the jokes.
S0.think: I think it would suit me fine. I don't use AI tools, and if it fizzles I keep doing what I know, which is what I want.
S0.do: Keeps running the corrugator on the same day shifts. Asks again about the senior pay grade she's been promised for three years.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, though she wasn't very worried to start with.
S0.quote: I'm starting to think next year is a place, not a time.
S0.fieldNote: Lena is dry, practical and attached to her machine after nineteen years. Her real stress in the calm world is cash flow, especially her partner's contract bus work. She hates borrowing, which matters for how she'd respond to bigger shocks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, let's see what actually comes. Everyone said the self-checkouts would end shop work and there are still people in shops. I'd keep my head down and do my job well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a corrugator's a beast. A computer could set it, maybe, but you need hands when a roll splits. I'd guess they'd keep me but cut the helpers, and I'd be doing the work of three with sensors watching me. That doesn't fill me with joy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to save a bit more, like fifty a fortnight, which is about what I can find. I wouldn't do a course unless they made me. I'd wait and see what they actually bring in, then deal with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when you hear a new noise in the machine and you're not sure yet if it's anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't do a course unless they made you. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not good at classrooms. I did my diploma at twenty and I was glad to be done. And when would I go? I start at six, I'm home by three for Max, and then it's dinner and homework. I'd rather be good at one thing than bad at two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kev, my helper at the wet end. He's thirty, two little ones, and his whole job is splicing rolls and clearing jams. If they bring in an auto-splicer, that's his job. He's a good lad. He'd probably end up at the warehouse on the motorway, nights.

S1.say: I'd say let's see what actually comes, like the self-checkouts that didn't end shop work. I'd keep my head down and do my job well.
S1.think: I think a computer might set the corrugator, but you still need hands when a roll splits. They'd keep me but cut the helpers, and I'd be doing the work of three under sensors.
S1.do: Saves about fifty every two weeks, which is what she can find. Avoids courses unless required and waits to see what the plant brings in before acting.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like hearing a new noise in the machine and not knowing yet if it matters.
S1.quote: I'd rather be good at one thing than bad at two.
S1.fieldNote: Lena trusts her own hands-on value and expects to be kept while helpers go. Her resistance to retraining is partly temperament and partly time: early shifts, school pickup and homework. She thinks of her helper Kev with real concern but doesn't see a way to protect him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably not say much in public, to be honest. I'd tell people I'm sure it'll sort itself out. But I'd want the government to do something for the people it hits, and fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be terrified. Two years and the box plant has robots doing my job, and Paul's bus probably drives itself. We'd have nothing coming in and nothing saved. I don't know how you plan for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything at once, the phone contracts, the takeaway on Fridays, Sophie's dance. I'd ask my sister if we could lean on her if it came to it, which would hurt. And I'd look for anything that still needs a person, the care home, the hospital kitchen, cleaning, whatever's going, before everyone else does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I can't breathe. Like I'm already behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hate borrowing from your sister. Would you still do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's the kids or my pride, it's the kids. But I'd hate every minute of it. She'd be lovely about it, which would make it worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first week after you lost the job look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wake up at five out of habit with nowhere to go. I'd go through every bill and every account. I'd be at the job centre, or whatever's left of it, with three hundred other people from the plant. That's the bit that frightens me, all of us at once.

S2.say: In public I'd say I'm sure it'll sort itself out. I'd want the government to help the people hit, and fast.
S2.think: I think I'd be terrified: robots doing my job in two years, my partner's bus driving itself, and nothing saved. I don't know how you plan for that.
S2.do: Cuts phone contracts, the Friday takeaway and her daughter's dance class at once. Asks her sister for help if needed and rushes to find any work still needing a person, such as a care home, hospital kitchen or cleaning.
S2.feel: Like she can't breathe and is already behind.
S2.quote: I'd be at the job centre, or whatever's left of it, with three hundred other people from the plant.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario overwhelms Lena: both incomes in the house exposed, no savings, and no appetite for change. The gap between her public 'it'll sort itself out' and private terror is the widest so far. She'd put pride aside for her kids but would hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning and the company should tell us straight what's coming. I'd want them to say which jobs and when. I'm not one for protests, but I'd sign a petition if the union put one round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's still fast for someone like me. Five years and I'm forty-eight, with a machine that doesn't need me. I'd be hoping they keep one person on each line for safety, and that it's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save hard for the first few years. Cut the takeaways, keep the old car going, put whatever's left aside, maybe get to two months saved. Then wait and see. If they announce it, I'd look for work at the care home in town, which has always got a vacancy board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but slower. Like the machine's making that noise and it's getting louder every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see. Isn't five years enough to do something now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe it is. But I don't know what the something is. If you told me, go learn this exact thing and you'll be safe, I'd do it. Nobody can tell me that, so I'll save money, because money's the only thing I know works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sophie, who's thirteen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to work hard at school and pick something where people need people. She wants to be a vet. I'd say good, animals don't want robots. I don't know if that's true.

S3.say: I'd say five years is fair warning and the company should tell us straight which jobs go and when. I'd sign a union petition but I'm not one for protests.
S3.think: I think it's still fast for someone like me, out of work at forty-eight. I'd hope they keep one person per line for safety, and that it's me.
S3.do: Cuts takeaways, keeps the old car running and saves toward two months of expenses in the first few years. Waits for an announcement, then looks for work at the local care home.
S3.feel: Alarmed but slower, like a machine noise getting louder every week.
S3.quote: Nobody can tell me that, so I'll save money, because money's the only thing I know works.
S3.fieldNote: When challenged on waiting, Lena explained it well: she'd act if someone could tell her exactly what to learn. Lacking that, she falls back on saving, the one thing she trusts. She hopes to be the last person kept on the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and a lot can change. I'd tell people not to panic. Maybe I'd say the government should plan something for older workers, but I'd leave the shouting to others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is better, but it still lands when I'm fifty-three. That's too young to stop and too old to start again, if you ask me. I'd hope to scrape to the end of the mortgage, which is eleven years off, then deal with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd chip away at savings each month and try to overpay the mortgage a bit if we ever had a good month. I'd keep doing my job. With the kids, I'd be firmer about school, and I'd tell Sophie to get a skill with people in it. Then I'd watch and wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a background thing. It'd sit there every day, but I'd get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you could choose one thing to have ready by the time it lands, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage gone. If the house is ours, I can live on cleaning money or care-home money. If it isn't, I can't. That's the whole thing really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having ten years make you more willing to try something new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. Maybe a short course in something near the end, if the plant paid. But I'm not changing who I am at fifty. I'll be the woman who ran the corrugator till the last day they let her.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time and people shouldn't panic. Maybe the government should plan something for older workers, but I'd leave the shouting to others.
S4.think: I think it still lands at fifty-three, too young to stop and too old to start again. I'd hope to scrape to the end of the mortgage, eleven years away.
S4.do: Saves a little each month and overpays the mortgage in good months. Keeps doing her job, presses her children on school, and waits to see what happens.
S4.feel: A background anxiety that sits there every day while she gets on with things.
S4.quote: I'll be the woman who ran the corrugator till the last day they let her.
S4.fieldNote: For Lena, ten years comes down to one target: paying off the mortgage. She'd consider a short course only if the plant paid and only near the end. Her identity is tightly bound to her machine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. There'd be no time to do anything but panic. What would help is if the government helped people keep their homes, maybe paused mortgages for workers who lost their jobs to this. And someone actually telling us, plainly, which jobs are going and when.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the husbands and wives. Everyone thinks about their own job. But if Paul's bus goes too, that's two hits on one house. Nobody talks about that.

headlineQuote: I know when the paper's damp just by the sound it makes going over the rolls.
portrait: Lena Chen is a 43-year-old corrugator operator at a cardboard box plant, nineteen years on the same machine, who never uses AI tools. She's dry, practical and hates borrowing, and with her partner Paul on contract bus work, they live month to month with nothing saved. She shrugs off the AI Plateau and stays only uneasy about Steady Disruption, expecting to be kept while helpers go. AGI in 2 years throws her into panic because both household incomes are exposed. More time mostly changes how hard she can save, and her single goal with ten years is to pay off the mortgage before the end comes.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there'd be no time to do anything but panic.
whatWouldHelp: Government help for people to keep their homes, such as pausing mortgages for workers who lose jobs to AI, and plain information about which jobs are going and when.
